Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict — the push climbs to 20 N

Set the Applied force F slider to 20 N. The block (5 kg, μₛ = 0.5) resists with at most μₛmg = 24.5 N. The push ramps from 0 to 20 N and the block does not move. What is friction doing over that range?

2 · Watch — friction tracks the push

With F at 20 N — safely below the 24.5 N peak, so the block stays put — press ▶ Play. F ramps from 0 to 20 N. Watch the friction arrow on the LEFT: it grows in lockstep with the applied arrow, so the two exactly cancel. On the RIGHT, the working point climbs the f = F line. This is what a self-adjusting force LOOKS like.

3 · Predict — the instant F exceeds 24.5 N

You keep ramping. At F = 24.5 N the friction is at its maximum. Push a tiny bit harder — F = 24.6 N. What happens to the friction force at that instant?

4 · Explore

Set F back to 30 N and Play again — watch the graph climb the f = F line to the peak at μₛmg, then fall vertically to μₖmg. The gap between those two values is the size of the lurch. Change the mass or the coefficients and see how the peak and the drop rescale together. The one thing to remember: static friction is whatever cancels the push, right up to the moment it gives — and then it DROPS.

The Physics

Static to Kinetic — the Drop You Can Feel · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A block rests on a rough floor while a horizontal push builds up from zero. The sim draws the push and the friction as arrows and plots friction against push, so you can follow the force through the moment the block breaks free.

What you'll learn

  • How friction behaves on a block at rest while the push builds up.
  • How the largest friction at rest depends on the mass and on μₛ.
  • What happens to the friction when the block starts to slide, and where μₖ enters.
A block of mass m on a level floor, pushed with a horizontal force F. The two surfaces set μₛ and μₖ.

What's on screen

  • Push F: the amber arrow at the left of the block, drawn to a fixed scale in newtons.
  • Friction f: the green arrow under the block, on the same scale. A badge above reads STATIC or KINETIC.
  • Graph (right): friction f against applied force F. The amber dot is the working point.
See itRun the block with F set to 20 N. Watch for: the amber push arrow growing from zero while the block stays at rest.

Fixed: g = 9.81 m/s², a level floor, a horizontal push, and a push that ramps up at 8 N per second. A run ends when the block has moved 2 m.

03

Static friction matches the push while the block rests

If the block does not move, its acceleration is zero, so the net horizontal force is zero. Friction must therefore cancel the push exactly:

fₛ = F  (F ≤ μₛmg)
Static friction takes whatever value the push needs.

With F at 15 N, friction is 15 N. With F at 20 N, friction is 20 N. Static friction is a self-adjusting force: it grows with the push, newton for newton, instead of sitting at one fixed value.

On the graph the working point climbs the dashed 45° line, f = F, while the block stays still.

See itRun with F set to 15 N. Watch for: the friction readout rising to 15.00 N as the push does, with the regime still static.
04

Static friction has a ceiling of μₛmg

Static friction cannot grow forever. On a level floor the normal force is N = mg, and the largest static friction is

fₛ,max = μₛN = μₛmg
The formula "friction = μN" gives this maximum, not the friction at every moment.

With the opening values (m = 5 kg, μₛ = 0.5) the ceiling is 0.5 × 5 × 9.81 ≈ 24.5 N. Doubling the mass doubles it, and so does doubling μₛ.

A push below the ceiling never moves the block. For m = 10 kg and μₛ = 0.4 the ceiling is 39.2 N, so a push of 30 N leaves it at rest.

See itRun m = 10 kg, μₛ = 0.40 and F = 30 N. Watch for: the block staying at rest, with the peak in the readout at 39.24 N, above the 30 N push.
05

Friction drops at breakaway, from μₛmg to μₖmg

When the push passes μₛmg the block slips. From then on the surfaces slide against each other, and the friction is the kinetic value:

fk = μₖmg  (μₖ ≤ μₛ)
Kinetic friction does not depend on the size of the push.

Since μₖ is smaller than μₛ, friction falls suddenly at that instant. At the opening values it goes from 24.5 N down to 0.3 × 5 × 9.81 ≈ 14.7 N, a drop of about 9.8 N. On the graph the working point leaves the f = F line and drops straight down.

In this sim fk stays constant while the block slides, whatever its speed.

See itRun the opening values, F = 30 N. Watch for: friction climbing to 24.5 N, then falling to 14.7 N as the badge switches to KINETIC and the block moves off.
06

The block lurches because the net force jumps

Just before breakaway the net force on the block is zero. Just after, friction has fallen by (μₛ − μₖ)mg and the push has not, so the net force suddenly equals that drop. Once the block moves, Newton's second law gives

a = (F − μₖmg) / m
Just after breakaway, F ≈ μₛmg.

At that moment a = (μₛ − μₖ)g, which is 0.2 × 9.81 ≈ 2.0 m/s² for the opening values, whatever the mass. So the block does not creep away: it starts with a definite jolt. If μₖ equals μₛ there is no drop and the start is gentle.

These numbers follow the sim's sliders.

See itRun F = 30 N with μₖ raised to 0.50, equal to μₛ. Watch for: Drop at breakaway reading 0.00 N, and no vertical step on the graph.
07

Where it matters

  • Moving furniture. A heavy wardrobe needs a larger push to start moving than to keep moving, because μₛ is usually larger than μₖ. Once it slips, friction falls and the same push accelerates it.
  • Stick-slip. A violin bow, a squeaking door hinge and chalk on a board repeatedly stick, slip and stick again. Each cycle is a jump between a static and a kinetic friction value.
  • Tyres. A rolling tyre grips the road with static friction. A wheel that locks and skids falls back to the lower kinetic value, so braking is weaker. Anti-lock brakes release the brakes briefly to stop the wheels locking.
  • Walking. Your shoe does not slide on the ground as you push back on it, so the force that moves you forward is static friction.
08

Summary

In one line. Friction on a block follows one rule while it rests and another once it slides, and the sim lets you push through the change and read the force.

Key points

  • At rest, fₛ = F, up to the ceiling fₛ,max = μₛmg.
  • Sliding, fk = μₖmg, no larger than μₛmg.
  • At breakaway friction drops by (μₛ − μₖ)mg, then a = (F − μₖmg)/m.

Common mix-ups

  • "Friction is always μN." μₛN is only the largest static friction. At rest friction equals the push; while sliding it is μₖN.
  • "A bigger push means more friction, even on a sliding block." Kinetic friction stays at μₖmg. A bigger push only raises the acceleration.
  • "Friction only acts when something moves." Static friction acts on a block at rest and holds it still.

Things to try on your own

  • With the opening values, set F to 24.5 N and then 25 N, and check each against the ceiling.
  • Set m = 10 kg and find the smallest F on the slider that moves the block.
  • Lower μₖ to 0.05 and compare the drop in the readout with the drop at 0.30.
